Figure 4: The distribution of loss gaps for the 10 clients for a heterogeneous split (α = 0.5) with CNN model. We notice that in the case of high non-iid data, EAGLE reduces the gap of the worst performing client in terms of loss and achieves less variance then other baselines.

Figure 3: Local losses and local gaps for EAGLE(λ = 2.0), q-FFL (q = 5.0) and AFL. The optimal local loss of client 0 is nearly 0 by design and thus only its loss gap is visible in the plot. By balancing the losses across clients, q-FFL and AFL prioritize learning a good classifier for clients 1 and 2, which harms the performance of client 0. In contrast, by balancing the loss gaps across clients, EAGLE allows all clients to benefit equally from federated learning.

Table 1: Performance of different algorithms on EMNIST with a highly heterogeneous split (α = 0.1) and a linear model. EAGLE achieves the best performance for the worst-performing client in terms of loss gaps, while maintaining accuracy comparable to the other baselines.

Table 2: Performance of different algorithms on DirtyMNIST with a CNN model. EAGLE achieves the best performance for the worst-performing client in terms of loss gaps, while slightly improving accuracy comparable to the other baselines. Note that all approaches generally achieve good accuracy because clients with ambiguous examples provide gradients that are also useful for the clean data.

Figure 5: Synthetic data distributions of the three clients. Rotating data resulted in client 1 and client 2 sharing the same optimal separator which is different than the one for client 0. This difference resuls in conflicting gradient directions between local optimizers for different clients.

Figure 6: Training behavior on the synthetic dataset. AFL and q-FFL increase the training loss of client 0 to match that of client 2, but fail to balance the losses of client 1 and client 2, which share the same optimal model despite differing in data separability.
